newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FEATURE - Czech Gypsies fight image as thieves.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Czech Gypsies fight image as thieves.

text.p: Ask many Czechs what they associate with Gypsies and the answer will be crime.
Some regard crime committed by the estimated 200,000-strong minority as a major problem, even when they rarely set eyes on a Gypsy, let alone witness a crime committed by them.
Community leaders admit that some Gypsies are involved in crime, mainly petty theft and pickpocketing, but proportionately no more than white Czechs.

The real issue, they say, is the depressingly common problems of minorities in Western societies: high unemployment, low education and bad health. Leaders call for U.S.-style affirmative action programmes to tackle these woes.
Such plans run foul of the prejudice against Gypsies common in central and eastern Europe, where the 1989 fall of communism has allowed long-suppressed racist views to be aired in public.
The leader of the far-right Czech Republican Party, Miroslav Sladek, used a parliamentary debate on the age of criminal responsibility in July to do just that.

"Just to show what people think about Gypsies, I can tell you from my experience what I have heard: "Gypsies should be punished from the time they were born because this is, in fact, their greatest crime'," he said.
Sladek's comments provoked a walkout by deputies of all parties except the little-reformed communists and his own.
But the Republicans' anti-Gypsy rhetoric has struck a chord with some Czechs, winning the party eight percent in elections earlier this year, up from six percent in 1992.
A recent Czech opinion poll showed that 29 percent of respondents admitted to disliking other races. Of those, two thirds felt most antipathy towards Gypsies.
Gypsies are also the victims of racially motivated attacks often by far-right skinheads, some of which end in murder.

Jiri Kanturek, spokesman for the opposition Social Democrats, criticises media reporting of crimes by Gypsies -- or Romanies as they are often called because the word "Gypsy" has a derogatory connotation in Czech.
"During our election campaign we would arrive at a village where there were no Romanies yet the population insisted that the biggest problem that they saw was Gypsy criminality.".
"The image of the world created by the media projects itself on to people's lives," he said.
But he said the Social Democrats, the biggest opposition party, had no policy for improving the lot of Gypsies.
Ivan Vesely, who leads a Gypsy foundation, says white Czechs are wrong to generalise about his people, who originated in India and started arriving in Europe generations ago.
For a start, the Gypsies are not a unified community. There are eight ethnicities worldwide and two groups in the Czech Republic: the "olasski" and the educated.

Vesely, president of the Foundation for Restoration and Development of Traditional Romany Values (DZENO), said the olasskis were the poorest members of the community with little or no education and therefore forced into crime and begging.

"It is wrong to judge our people as a whole," said Vesely, himself a Gypsy. "It is the olasski in general who steal but there are even differences within the olasski group. There are those among them with university education."
The olasski, who account for about 10 percent of Czech Gypsies, are named after an area of Romania from where they are reputed to have emigrated in the 18th century.
"What I think is important to mention is that even in the Czech population there are thieves and criminals," said Vesely.

While the Czech crime rate is low by international standards, there is evidence of widespread white-collar crime and corruption. Car theft, near epidemic proportions in the big cities, is not a Gypsy speciality.
Vesely plans to confront Sladek by demanding an apology and a symbolic 100 crowns in damages for every Czech Gypsy, although he does not expect the money to be paid.

Affirmative action, a controversial system in used in the United States to help minorities, should be applied in the Czech Republic, said Vesely. Under this, education and work places were reserved for minorities.

"It is essential that Gypsies be given qualifications that will later cut their unemployment," he said. "Conditions must (also) be established for the development of Gypsy culture and self-identity, for instance theatre, literature, film..."

Jitka Gjuricova, a departmental director at the Interior Ministry, is gloomy. "I visted the USA with its affirmative action programmes and I am still pessimistic about the possibility of mutual acceptance of different ethnicities."
But she said things were improving even though the problem might seem worse because of the public airing of an issue stifled before the 1989 "Velvet Revolutiom" ended communism.

"I even think that the worst is over. Now we are developing new ways of dealing with the problem," she said. "The Gypsy problem was not born with the revolution. After the revolution it was only made public."
